1 What stability means, informally

In the time response of linear systems, we looked at the stabilities of different trajectories without ever defining stability formally.

So what does stability actually mean?

We will start with an informal definition.

Roughly, a stable trajectory of a possibly nonlinear dynamic system is one for which a small perturbation of the initial condition leads to perturbations that stay small.

Importantly, notice that the following two things are easy to skip past, and both matter.

The definition is about a trajectory, not about a system, so the same system can have one stable trajectory and one unstable one.

It is also a statement about all future time, not about what happens over the next few seconds.

Question: why is it wrong to call a whole nonlinear system "stable" without saying more?

A nonlinear system can have many equilibria and many nominal trajectories, each with its own stability.

The pendulum is the standard example, with the hanging position stable and the inverted position unstable.

Both are equilibria of the same set of equations, so the system by itself is neither stable nor unstable.

For a linear time-invariant system the distinction collapses, because every trajectory shares the same eigenvalues, which is why the loose phrasing is harmless there.

2 Lyapunov stability

Consider the nonlinear system together with a nominal solution.

The nominal solution is stable in the sense of Lyapunov if the following holds.

Definition: Lyapunov stability

A single never has to work for every , and for a time-varying system it may depend on as well.

Notice that comes first, and is only found afterwards, once an has been given.

You name a tolerance tube of radius , and stability means someone can always find a starting ball of radius whose trajectories never leave that tube.

The norm

The norm used is the ordinary two-norm.

The nominal solution is usually an equilibrium

Very often the nominal solution is just an equilibrium point.

Lyapunov stability is weak

It guarantees that a small perturbation of the initial condition results in small perturbations of the trajectory.

In control we usually want the perturbation to go to zero, which is what asymptotic stability requires, and that definition is introduced in Section 3.

Question 1: what would go wrong if the quantifiers were swapped, so that a single had to work for every ?

Nothing but the equilibrium itself would qualify.

Since may be taken arbitrarily small, a fixed would have to keep every trajectory in a ball of radius smaller than any positive number.

That forces the trajectory to sit exactly on the nominal solution forever, which is a useless definition.

Writing makes the dependence explicit and is what allows genuine motion inside the tube.

Question 2: why does the definition allow to depend on as well?

Dependence on is essential, since a tighter tube naturally demands a tighter starting ball.

Dependence on matters for time-varying systems, where the same perturbation applied at different moments can grow by different amounts.

When a single works for every , the property is called uniform stability, which is a stronger statement.

For a time-invariant system the two coincide, because shifting only shifts the time axis.

Question 3: the definition speaks of a nominal trajectory, not only an equilibrium. Why is that generality worth keeping?

Many aerospace problems have no useful equilibrium to talk about.

An orbit, a landing approach and a coordinated turn are all trajectories, and the question is whether the vehicle stays near the planned one.

The trick is to define the error and study its dynamics.

Linearising this about the nominal trajectory gives a linear time-varying system in the error.

Stability of the nominal trajectory then becomes a question about the state transition matrix of that error system.

Question 4: why does the two-norm get used rather than some other measure of size?

Mostly convenience, because in finite dimensions the choice does not change the answer.

All norms on are equivalent, meaning any two are within constant factors of each other.

Rescaling and by those constants converts a proof in one norm into a proof in the other.

The two-norm is preferred because it comes from an inner product, which makes the quadratic Lyapunov functions used later behave nicely.

3 Asymptotic stability

Instead of Lyapunov stability, what control engineers usually want is that the perturbation not merely stay small but actually die out, and strengthening the definition in that way gives asymptotic stability.

The nominal solution is asymptotically stable if two separate things hold.

Condition (a) is that it is stable in the sense of Lyapunov.

Condition (b) is a convergence requirement, and it carries its own radius .

Definition: asymptotic stability

Both halves are required, since (a) alone allows a permanent oscillation and (b) alone allows an arbitrarily large excursion before the return.

In words, the perturbation stays small and it also goes to zero as .

The radius plays a different role from : is found in response to a given tolerance , while is tied to no tolerance and describes how close you must start for convergence to be promised.

Question 1: in the definition of Lyapunov stability, depends on . In the definition of asymptotic stability, depends on nothing but . Why the difference?

The two conditions answer different questions.

The condition is about how far the trajectory may stray, so it must adapt to whatever tube radius you demand.

The condition is about whether the trajectory returns at all, and that is a yes or no question with no tolerance attached.

The set of initial conditions satisfying is a region of attraction, and its size is a property of the system rather than a parameter you choose.

Question 2: a satellite spins about a principal axis with no damping, so the nominal solution is a constant spin rate. A small torque impulse changes that rate slightly. Which of conditions (a) and (b) does the resulting motion satisfy, and which one fails?

It satisfies Lyapunov stability but not the convergence condition.

A small torque impulse changes the spin rate by a small amount, and with no dissipation that change persists forever.

The perturbation stays small, which is condition (a), but it never returns to zero, so condition (b) fails.

This is exactly the situation a momentum management controller is added to fix, and it is the practical reason the difference between the two definitions matters.

Question 3: give a system that is Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable.

An undamped oscillator, which is a harmonic oscillator with no friction.

Every trajectory is a closed ellipse around the origin, so a small starting displacement gives a small orbit forever.

That satisfies the Lyapunov definition, with proportional to .

But nothing converges to the origin, so it fails asymptotic stability.

Question 4: can a trajectory converge to the equilibrium and still fail to be asymptotically stable?

Yes, and this is why the two conditions are stated separately.

Here is the standard example, with the state confined to the unit circle and written in terms of the angle.

The only equilibrium is , which is the point .

Since , with equality only at the equilibrium itself, increases monotonically, and the solution is available in closed form.

Every trajectory therefore travels once around the circle and returns to , so condition (b) holds for every initial condition, with as large as you like.

The distance from the equilibrium along the way is available in closed form too.

Whatever you start from, that distance passes through when the trajectory reaches the far side of the circle, which is the diameter and the largest separation available.

Started a distance from , with . The trajectory converges to , yet it first swings out to a distance of , and shrinking only delays that excursion rather than shrinking it.

So the convergence condition is satisfied while the Lyapunov condition is not, because for any no keeps the excursion below .

Such an equilibrium is called attractive but not stable, and asymptotic stability rules it out by demanding both properties.

For linear time-invariant systems this cannot happen, since convergence of every trajectory already forces all eigenvalues to have negative real parts.

D1 Demo: Lyapunov stability, delta and epsilon

This demo acts out the definition of Lyapunov stability, with the origin as the nominal solution.

Every system in the menu is linear and time invariant, , and only the matrix changes from one choice to the next.

Reading the stability of each one off is exactly what the later sections do, starting with Section 8, so for now just watch what the trajectories do.

A ring of initial conditions of radius is released, and the demo measures the largest distance from the origin that any of them reaches.

For a stable choice that largest distance is the smallest valid . For an unstable one it only reflects the horizon you selected, since no finite works.

State plane: the starting ball and the reached set
Distance from the origin against time

Left plot: the cyan circle is the starting ball of radius , the purple circle is the smallest tube radius that contains every trajectory over the simulated horizon, the red curves are the trajectories themselves, and the orange dots mark where they are at the current instant of the animation. The navy dot at the centre is the equilibrium. Right plot: the norm for each trajectory against time, with the cyan dashed line at and the purple dashed line at .

Question 1: for the stable spiral, halve and watch . What relationship do you find, and why is it exact for a linear system?

The value of halves as well, so the ratio stays fixed.

Linearity is the reason: scaling the initial condition scales the whole trajectory by the same factor.

The ratio itself has a name, and it is the largest transient amplification of the system.

For nonlinear systems no such proportionality exists, which is exactly why the definition allows to depend on in an arbitrary way.

Question 2: compare the stable spiral with the undamped centre. Both satisfy the definition, so what does the right plot show as the difference?

For the spiral, every norm curve decays towards zero.

For the centre, the norm curves oscillate forever between fixed bounds and never approach zero.

Both stay inside the purple line, so both are Lyapunov stable.

Only the spiral is asymptotically stable, since only it satisfies the extra convergence condition.

Note also that the centre's norm is not constant unless the trajectories are circles, because the ellipses traced by the state have different distances from the origin at different points.

Question 3: select the defective marginal case. Its eigenvalues both sit at zero, so why is it unstable?

This system is the double integrator, whose state matrix is a single Jordan block at zero.

The exponential factor is one, so nothing decays, and the polynomial factor grows without bound.

Any initial condition with drifts away forever, so no finite can contain the trajectory.

This is why the eigenvalue table of Case II in Section 8 requires marginal eigenvalues to be non-defective, and it is a very real case: an uncontrolled spacecraft attitude axis behaves exactly like this.

5 Global and local asymptotic stability

Without loss of generality take , since a time invariant system does not care where the clock starts.

Globally asymptotically stable

The system is globally asymptotically stable, written G.A.S., if every trajectory converges to the equilibrium.

This is the case arbitrarily large, and it forces to be the unique equilibrium of the system.

Locally asymptotically stable

The system is locally asymptotically stable, written L.A.S., near if there exists some for which the following holds.

A nonlinear system can have several equilibrium points, so local is the only honest statement in general.

Why G.A.S. forces uniqueness of the equilibrium point: if a second equilibrium existed, the trajectory starting exactly at would sit there forever and never reach , which contradicts the definition.

A linear system is the special case where the distinction between G.A.S. and L.A.S. collapses, along with the dependence on the nominal trajectory.

The linear special case

For nonlinear systems we must always name the nominal trajectory whose stability is in question.

For a linear system that qualification disappears, and below we see why.

Take the linear, possibly time varying system and any nominal trajectory of it.

Define the perturbation as the difference between the two.

Differentiate and substitute.

The perturbation obeys the same equation as the state, no matter which nominal trajectory you picked.

Therefore if one nominal trajectory is stable then all of them are.

Main result

Stability is a property of the linear system rather than of one of its trajectories, so studying the zero solution settles it for every trajectory at once.

Where linearity is used: the step is exactly the distributive property of a linear map. For a nonlinear the difference depends on where sits, which is the whole reason nonlinear stability is local.

Question 1: a ball rolls in the landscape drawn below, which has two valleys separated by a hill. Classify each of the three equilibria.

The landscape is the double well , whose equilibria are the two valley bottoms at and the hilltop at .

Each valley bottom in the plot is locally asymptotically stable when there is friction, since a ball released nearby rolls down and settles there, exactly as the dashed arrow shows.

Neither valley is globally asymptotically stable, because the shaded strip under the curve splits the positions in two: a ball released to the left of the hilltop reaches the left valley and never the right one.

The hilltop at is an unstable equilibrium, since any perturbation grows and sends the ball down one side or the other, which is why it is the watershed between the two shaded regions.

Without friction the valley bottoms would only be Lyapunov stable, because the ball would roll up the far side to the same height and oscillate forever.

The set of initial conditions that reach a given valley is called its region of attraction, and it is almost never a ball: for a nonlinear system its boundary is usually curved and can be fractal, while the definition of L.A.S. only asks for some ball of radius to fit inside it.

Question 2: can a system be globally asymptotically stable and still be badly behaved in practice?

Yes, because G.A.S. says nothing about how far the state travels or how long it takes.

A trajectory may grow by orders of magnitude before it turns around, which can saturate actuators or break the modelling assumptions.

It may also converge arbitrarily slowly, since the definition contains a limit but no rate.

This is why practical specifications add settling time, overshoot and a decay rate on top of the qualitative property.

Question 3: why does L.A.S. imply G.A.S. for a linear system but not for a nonlinear one?

Because a linear system is scale invariant.

If is a solution then so is for any constant .

So convergence from a small ball automatically extends to the whole space by rescaling.

A nonlinear system has no such symmetry, and the double well demo below, Demo D2, shows a case where doubling the initial condition changes which equilibrium you reach.

Question 4: the derivation used a time varying . Does anything about it require time invariance?

No, the cancellation works for any , so the conclusion covers linear time varying systems too.

What does not carry over is the eigenvalue test of Section 8.

There are time varying systems whose has eigenvalues in the left half plane at every instant and which are nevertheless unstable.

For those you need the state transition matrix rather than a snapshot of the eigenvalues.

Question 5: an aircraft is flying a coordinated turn, which is a nominal trajectory rather than an equilibrium. How does the stability study of a linear system help?

Linearize the nonlinear aircraft model about the turn to get an error system.

That error system is linear, so the main result above applies to it: its stability is a property of the error system itself and not of which error you happen to start with, and testing the zero solution settles every case.

If the turn is flown at a constant rate the linearization is time invariant, and the eigenvalue test of Section 8 applies directly.

This is the standard route from a nonlinear flight model to a linear design.

This demo uses a damped double well oscillator, which is the ball in the landscape from the question above.

There are three equilibria, at , and .

A grid of initial conditions is simulated and each one is coloured by the equilibrium it reaches, which paints the two regions of attraction.

State plane: regions of attraction and the probe trajectory
Distance from each equilibrium against time

Left plot: each small dot is one initial condition, purple when its trajectory ends at and cyan when it ends at . The two green dots are the stable equilibria, the red hollow circle at the origin is the unstable one, the black cross marks the starting point set by the probe sliders, and the amber curve is the trajectory from that point. Right plot: the distance from the probe trajectory to each of the two stable equilibria against time, drawn in the same purple and cyan, so the curve that reaches zero identifies the winner.

Question 1: move the probe slowly across the boundary between the two colours. What happens to the trajectory near the crossing?

The trajectory heads towards the origin, lingers near it, and then falls into one well or the other.

The boundary is made of the trajectories that converge exactly to the saddle at the origin, which is its stable manifold.

Starting on the boundary itself the state would approach the origin and stay there, but the slightest error to one side decides the outcome.

This is the nonlinear version of the stable subspace idea, and it explains why the outcome is so sensitive right at the crossing.

Question 2: increase the damping towards its maximum. Why do the regions become simpler?

With heavy damping the state loses energy quickly and cannot cross the central hill.

Each region of attraction then reduces to roughly the half plane containing its own well, with a nearly straight boundary.

With light damping the state can swing over the hill several times before settling, so the boundary curls into thin interleaved bands.

Those bands are why a region of attraction is generally impossible to describe with a simple formula.

Question 3: is either well globally asymptotically stable, and is either one locally asymptotically stable?

Neither is globally asymptotically stable, because the other colour occupies a large part of the plane.

Both are locally asymptotically stable, since a small enough ball around each one lies entirely inside its own colour.

The Jacobian at confirms this.

Its eigenvalues have negative real parts for every , which is the indirect method, covered later on this page, applied ahead of schedule.

D3 Demo: the perturbation ignores the nominal trajectory, a linear system

This demo checks that claim by running several nominal trajectories at once.

Each nominal trajectory gets a companion trajectory offset by the same fixed perturbation vector, and the demo plots the difference.

The linear case gives one single curve for the perturbation, while the nonlinear case gives a family of different curves.

State plane: nominal trajectories and their perturbed twins
Size of the perturbation against time, logarithmic scale

Left plot: solid navy curves are the nominal trajectories , dashed red curves are the perturbed trajectories started from , and the green dots mark the starting points. Right plot: one curve per pair, showing against time, on a logarithmic vertical axis, so pure exponential growth or decay appears as a straight line and two curves differing by a constant factor appear as the same shape shifted vertically. For a linear model every curve lies on top of the others, so you see a single thick line. The readout gives the spread between the curves as a percentage.

Question 1: for the two linear models the curves collapse onto one. What does that single curve depend on?

Only on the matrix and on the perturbation itself.

The nominal trajectory has cancelled completely, which is the algebraic fact proved above.

Changing the perturbation size rescales the whole curve, because the map is linear.

Question 2: for the pendulum the curves separate. What does the spread depend on?

On where each nominal trajectory happens to be in the state space.

For a nonlinear model the perturbation still obeys an exact equation, but the nominal no longer cancels out of it.

When the perturbation is small the right hand side is well approximated by its linearization, which is the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives of evaluated on the nominal trajectory.

Near the hanging position the Jacobian is stable and the error shrinks quickly.

Near the inverted position it has a positive eigenvalue and the error grows, which is why the curves fan out.

Question 3: shrink the perturbation size for the nonlinear models. Do the curves come back together?

No. Drag the perturbation slider down and watch the right plot: every curve slides down the logarithmic axis by roughly the same amount and keeps its shape, but they stay a family of separate curves rather than merging into one.

The readout says the same thing numerically. The spread stays near 50 percent for the pendulum and close to 100 percent for the double well however small you make the perturbation, while either linear model stays below 0.5 percent at every setting.

The reason is the approximate error equation from Question 2, in which the Jacobian is evaluated on the nominal trajectory.

Shrinking the perturbation makes that approximation more accurate, since it is the higher order terms that get removed, but it does nothing to itself, which still differs from one nominal trajectory to the next. That is what keeps the curves apart.

For the two linear models the same Jacobian is at every point of the state space, which is exactly why their curves coincide instead.

What you do gain is proportionality: halving the perturbation halves every curve, and on a logarithmic axis that is a rigid downward shift of the whole family.

8 LTI stability: the eigenvalue test

Case I: a full set of eigenvectors

Consider the unforced time invariant system.

Case I is the situation where has a full set of eigenvectors, so it is diagonalizable.

The response then has the modal decomposition of a diagonalizable system.

Here are the eigenvectors of and are the rows of , which are the left eigenvectors.

Every term is a fixed direction scaled by the scalar , so the whole question of stability reduces to the sign of .

The three cases

Case 1: if for ALL , the system is asymptotically stable.

Case 2: if for ANY , the system is unstable.

Case 3: if for ALL , the system is Lyapunov stable.

Main result

With a full set of eigenvectors the whole question is decided by the signs of the real parts, since each mode is a fixed direction scaled by .

Read the words carefully: Case 1 needs ALL eigenvalues in the open left half plane, while Case 2 needs only ONE in the open right half plane. A single bad mode ruins the whole system, because its direction is present in almost every initial condition.

Question 1: for a stable linear system, how does relate to in the Lyapunov definition?

They are simply proportional, because the response is linear in the initial condition.

Calling that supremum , the choice always works.

The constant is the largest transient amplification of the system, and it can be much bigger than one even when every eigenvalue is stable.

Demo D1 measures exactly this ratio.

Question 2: two systems have identical eigenvalues at . Can one of them behave much worse than the other?

Yes, over the transient, even though both are asymptotically stable with the same decay rate.

The eigenvalues fix the long run behaviour, but the eigenvectors fix how much the response grows on the way there.

When the eigenvectors are nearly parallel, is large and the bound allows a big excursion before the decay takes over.

Such matrices are called non-normal, and the effect matters in practice, since a large transient can drive a real system into saturation or into a region where the linearization no longer holds.

Question 3: a system has eigenvalues at and , with two independent eigenvectors. What is the verdict?

Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable, which is Case 3.

The mode at decays and the mode at holds its value.

The trajectory stays bounded and close to the origin, so the Lyapunov condition holds, but it settles at rather than at zero.

A single integrator behaves this way, and it is a very common situation in practice.

Case II: repeated eigenvalues

Case II is when has repeated eigenvalues and does not have eigenvectors.

A more general modal decomposition is needed, built from the Jordan transformation.

The columns are the eigenvectors and generalized eigenvectors associated with the eigenvalue .

The inverse supplies the matching left vectors.

The response in modal form is then a triple sum.

The boxed factor is the only new ingredient, and it is where the polynomial in enters.

The fastest growing term

For each eigenvalue the most rapidly growing term goes like the following.

So if but , this term grows even though the real part is zero.

The three cases, restated

Case 1: if for ALL , the system is asymptotically stable.

The exponential always wins against any fixed power of , which is why a Jordan block is harmless in the left half plane.

Case 2: if for ANY , the system is unstable.

Case 3: if for ALL , and for each with the number of associated eigenvectors equals the multiplicity of , then the system is Lyapunov stable.

Main result

The only change from Case I is the extra requirement on the marginal eigenvalues, which must be non-defective for the polynomial factor to be absent.

The underlined condition: a marginal eigenvalue is only safe when it is non-defective, meaning its Jordan blocks are all of size one. Eigenvalues strictly inside the left half plane are allowed to be defective, and eigenvalues in the right half plane are fatal either way.

Question 4: an eigenvalue at has a Jordan block of size 5. Is the system asymptotically stable, and does the block matter at all?

It is asymptotically stable, because .

The block still matters, because it creates a large transient before the decay takes over.

The response therefore keeps growing for the first 40 seconds before it starts to fall.

Asymptotic stability is a statement about the limit and says nothing about that excursion.

Question 5: two matrices both have with multiplicity two. Why is one Lyapunov stable and the other unstable?

Because they differ in the number of eigenvectors, which is exactly the condition in Case 3.

Here every vector is an eigenvector, the multiplicity is matched, and the state simply stays where it started.

Here there is only one eigenvector, the block has size two, and the entry grows without bound.

Question 6: where does a defective imaginary eigenvalue turn up in engineering practice?

In resonance, when an undamped oscillator is driven at exactly its natural frequency.

Modelling the drive as a second undamped oscillator in series produces a repeated pair with a Jordan block.

The amplitude then grows linearly in time, which is the classical resonance envelope.

The double integrator is the same phenomenon at , and an uncontrolled spacecraft attitude axis is a real example.

Three examples and the Hurwitz definition

Three small matrices hit all three cases.

Example 1: asymptotically stable

Characteristic polynomial

Verdict

Both real parts are negative, so the system is asymptotically stable.

Example 2: Lyapunov stable

Characteristic polynomial

Eigenvectors

Verdict

There are two eigenvectors for an eigenvalue of multiplicity two, so the marginal eigenvalue is non-defective.

The system is Lyapunov stable and not asymptotically stable.

Example 3: unstable

Characteristic polynomial

Eigenvectors

Verdict

Only one eigenvector for a multiplicity of two, so the marginal eigenvalue is defective.

The system is unstable even though no eigenvalue has a positive real part.

A couple of notes

For an LTI system, L.A.S. implies G.A.S.

An LTI system is G.A.S. to the origin if and only if all zeros of lie in the strict left half plane of the complex plane.

Definition: Hurwitz

A matrix is called Hurwitz if all eigenvalues of have negative real parts.

Definition: Hurwitz

For an LTI system the implication runs both ways, so Hurwitz and G.A.S. are two names for the same situation. Hurwitz remains a property of a matrix or a polynomial, and stability a property of a system, which is why the two words are kept apart.

The forward direction is Case 1 above. The converse holds as well, and it takes two lines.

Suppose the system is G.A.S. and let be any eigenvalue with eigenvector . Starting from gives a solution whose size is fixed by the real part alone.

If that norm never decays, so this trajectory does not converge to the origin and the system is not G.A.S.

Every eigenvalue must therefore satisfy , which is exactly the statement that is Hurwitz.

Question 7: Examples 2 and 3 have the same characteristic polynomial. What extra computation separated them?

Counting the eigenvectors of the repeated eigenvalue, which is a rank computation.

For Example 2, has rank 0, giving two eigenvectors.

For Example 3 the same matrix has rank 1, giving only one eigenvector.

The polynomial is blind to this, which is why the Jordan form is needed for the marginal case.

Question 8: is every Hurwitz matrix a matrix with negative diagonal entries?

No, and neither implication holds in either direction.

A matrix can be Hurwitz with a positive diagonal entry.

A matrix can also have both diagonal entries negative and still be unstable.

What is true is that the trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues, so a positive trace guarantees instability.

Question 9: why keep a separate word for Hurwitz instead of just saying stable?

Because Hurwitz is a property of a matrix while stability is a property of a system.

The same word then transfers cleanly to polynomials, where a Hurwitz polynomial is one with all roots in the open left half plane.

It also avoids ambiguity, since stable alone could mean Lyapunov stable, which permits eigenvalues on the axis.

The Routh-Hurwitz test of Section 11 is a test for exactly this property of a polynomial.

Place the eigenvalues wherever you like and watch the verdict and the response change together.

Complex plane: where the eigenvalues sit
Free response from a fixed initial condition

Left plot: the blue crosses are the eigenvalues, the vertical dashed purple line is the imaginary axis, and the shaded green band on the left is the strict left half plane where asymptotic stability lives. Right plot: the two state components against time in blue and green, together with the amber dashed envelope that the modal decomposition predicts.

Question 1: set the real part to exactly zero with a nonzero imaginary part. Which of the three cases is this, and what does the response look like?

This is Case 3, Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable.

The response is a pure sinusoid of constant amplitude, so the envelope is flat.

The two eigenvalues are distinct, so there are two independent eigenvectors and no polynomial factor appears.

That last point is what separates this harmless marginal case from the defective one of Case II in Section 8.

Question 2: switch to two real eigenvalues and put one at and the other at . Why does the response look stable at first?

Because the fast stable mode dominates the early part of the response.

The first term collapses within a couple of seconds while the second has barely moved.

The slow unstable mode takes about seconds to become visible, so a short simulation would hide it completely.

Lengthen the horizon slider and the growth appears, which is a good reminder that a simulation is not a stability proof.

Question 3: turn on the logarithmic axis with a stable complex pair. What shape does the envelope take, and why is that useful?

The envelope becomes a straight line, because a logarithm turns an exponential into a linear function.

The slope of that line is proportional to , so you can read the decay rate straight off the plot.

This is the standard way to measure a damping rate from experimental data, since the eigenvalue is not directly observable.

D5 Demo: defective against non-defective marginal modes

Every entry in the menu is an LTI system whose eigenvalues all lie on the imaginary axis, so for every and no eigenvalue is in the open left or the open right half plane.

A test that looked only at the real parts would therefore return the same verdict for all four, and for two of them that verdict would be wrong.

What separates them is how many eigenvectors each repeated eigenvalue has. Write for the algebraic multiplicity of , meaning its multiplicity as a root of , and for its geometric multiplicity, meaning the number of independent eigenvectors it has.

The eigenvalue is called defective when , that is when it has fewer eigenvectors than its multiplicity.

The criterion the demo illustrates is Case 3 of the eigenvalue test, stated in Section 8.

If instead a marginal eigenvalue is defective, the matrix exponential carries a polynomial factor that no exponential is left to cancel, and some solution is unbounded.

Two of the four systems below are non-defective and two are defective, and the readout under the plots prints , the pair and for the marginal eigenvalue, and the initial condition used for the simulation.

For a non-defective marginal eigenvalue the exponent is zero and the envelope is the constant . Right plot: the norm in green, with a purple dashed horizontal line at the initial norm . Question 1: compare the first two entries. Both have , so why do they behave differently?

The characteristic polynomial only records the eigenvalues and their multiplicities.

It cannot see how many independent eigenvectors belong to each eigenvalue, and that is the deciding factor here.

For the zero matrix, , so and the geometric multiplicity matches the algebraic one.

For the Jordan block, , so while , and the marginal eigenvalue is defective.

That is precisely the second requirement of Case 3, which asks for at every eigenvalue on the imaginary axis. The first requirement, , holds for both matrices, so the eigenvector count is the only thing separating them, and for the Jordan block the test returns no certificate of Lyapunov stability.

The system is not merely uncertified, it is genuinely unstable, and the matrix exponential shows why.

Every initial condition with grows without bound, however small it is, so no keeps the trajectory inside a given ball and the Lyapunov definition fails.

Question 2: the last entry is a resonant pair. What is the growth rate of its envelope?

Linear in time, because the Jordan block has size two and .

The oscillation itself does not decay or grow, since .

All the growth comes from the polynomial factor produced by the block.

Doubling the horizon therefore doubles the peak amplitude, which you can check with the slider.

Question 3: the third entry has a repeated pair at and is still Lyapunov stable. How is that consistent with the second entry being unstable?

The third entry is two identical but uncoupled oscillators.

Each eigenvalue has multiplicity two and also has two independent eigenvectors, one from each oscillator.

The defective version couples them, which is the block structure that creates the factor.

Repetition of an eigenvalue is never the problem on its own, only repetition without enough eigenvectors.

11 The Routh-Hurwitz test and the Routh array

The Routh-Hurwitz test

This section answers a practical question: can we decide whether is Hurwitz without computing any eigenvalues?

Start from the characteristic polynomial written with descending powers.

Construct the Hurwitz matrix.

The rule for entry is simple once you see it.

The test

When , the matrix is Hurwitz if and only if all the leading principal minors of are positive.

Routh-Hurwitz test

The verdict comes from the coefficients of alone, with no eigenvalue ever computed.

The test involves computing determinants.

The quick necessary condition

A necessary condition, which is not sufficient, is that every coefficient is positive.

This can be used to quickly tell when a system is unstable.

How to use the necessary condition: if any coefficient is negative or zero, stop, the polynomial is not Hurwitz. If all are positive you have learned nothing yet and must continue with the minors.

Question 1: for write the full test in terms of the coefficients.

With the three minors are the following.

Given , the conditions reduce to , and .

The middle coefficient is then positive automatically, which is worth noticing.

Question 2: give a polynomial with all coefficients positive that is not Hurwitz.

The standard one is a cubic where the product is too small.

All four coefficients are positive, so the necessary condition passes.

The test therefore fails, and indeed the roots are and .

It is the default setting of Demo D6 below, where lowering below one moves the pair back across the axis.

The Routh array

An equivalent approach avoids the determinants entirely and uses a table instead.

The rows are labelled by descending powers of , and the first two rows are just the coefficients split into even and odd positions.

Each new row is built by cross multiplying the two rows above it.

The same pattern then uses the previous two rows to make the , the and so on.

Missing coefficients are replaced by zeros, and the array is generated until the th row is complete.

The test

The matrix is Hurwitz if and only if all are positive and all entries of the first column are positive.

Routh array test

Same verdict as the leading minors, obtained by cross multiplication instead of determinants.

Worked example: the general cubic

The array

The conditions

These are the same two conditions the Hurwitz minors produced, which is the sense in which the two methods are equivalent.

Extra information for free: the number of sign changes down the first column equals the number of roots with positive real part. The Hurwitz minors give a yes or no answer, while the array also counts how many roots are misbehaving.

Question 3: the array needs and to continue. What does a zero in the first column mean?

It means the polynomial is not Hurwitz, since the test demands strictly positive entries.

It also signals a special case, because the division that builds the next row breaks down.

The usual repair is to replace the zero by a small positive and continue, then take the limit as .

An entire row of zeros is a different case and indicates roots that are symmetric about the origin, typically a pair on the imaginary axis.

Question 4: why does the array need only about multiplications while the minors need determinants?

The array is a Gaussian elimination in disguise, so each entry is computed once and reused.

Computing the minors separately repeats almost all of the same arithmetic times.

In fact the first column entries are ratios of consecutive Hurwitz minors.

That identity explains why positivity of the first column is the same statement as positivity of all the minors.

Question 5: a controller has gain and the closed loop polynomial is . For which is the loop stable?

Apply the two cubic conditions with , , and .

So the stable range is .

At the array has a zero in the first column and the roots are and .

This is the classic use of the test, since it gives a design range without ever solving for the roots.

Question 1: start from the default cubic and lower slowly. At what value does the verdict change, and what happens on the left plot?

The verdict flips when changes sign, which for happens at .

Exactly at that value the complex pair sits on the imaginary axis, at .

Below it the pair moves left and the polynomial is Hurwitz, above it the pair moves right and the polynomial is not.

This crossing is the beginning of the root locus idea.

Question 2: set negative while keeping the others positive. Which test catches it first?

The quick necessary condition catches it immediately, since a coefficient is no longer positive.

The minor also turns negative, so the full test agrees.

This is the practical value of the necessary condition, because it takes one glance rather than determinants.

It only ever proves instability, never stability.

Question 3: can you find a setting where all the coefficients are positive and the system is still unstable?

Yes, and the default setting is one of them.

All coefficients are positive but , and the roots include a pair with positive real part.

This shows the necessary condition is genuinely weaker than the test.

For degree 2 the two coincide, which is why the gap only becomes visible from degree 3 upwards.

Question 1: use the marginal preset. What does the first column do, and what do the roots do?

An entry in the first column becomes zero, so the test fails without any sign change.

The roots show a complex pair sitting exactly on the imaginary axis.

Zero sign changes means no roots strictly in the right half plane, which is consistent.

The polynomial is not Hurwitz, and whether the system is Lyapunov stable depends on whether that axis pair is defective, which the polynomial alone cannot tell you.

Question 2: raise the constant term with the scale slider on a stable preset. Which entry of the first column goes negative first?

For a cubic it is the entry, which is .

Raising makes the numerator negative while everything else stays fixed.

This produces two sign changes, one going down into the negative entry and one coming back up to .

Two sign changes means two roots in the right half plane, which matches the complex pair you see crossing over.

Question 3: why does the sign change count always come out even for a real polynomial with a complex pair crossing over?

Because complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs.

Both members of the pair have the same real part, so they cross the axis together.

An odd count therefore means a real root has crossed instead, which happens when the constant term changes sign.

Watching whether the count changes by one or by two tells you which kind of instability you are approaching.

14 Lyapunov's indirect method

Everything so far about the eigenvalue test applies to linear systems, so the question now is how to test a nonlinear system.

Recall the nonlinear system and pick one equilibrium state.

Step 1: perturb the initial state

Step 2: take the nominal to be the equilibrium

Now differentiate the perturbed state and expand in a Taylor series about .

The remainder is small in the precise sense that it vanishes faster than the perturbation itself.

Therefore the perturbed system satisfies the following equation.

Why a Hurwitz Jacobian is enough

Write evaluated at and use the variation of constants formula.

If is Hurwitz then , and because is negligible compared with the integral cannot sustain the perturbation either.

So the original nonlinear system is L.A.S. around the equilibrium .

Theorem

Theorem: Lyapunov's indirect method

Let be an equilibrium state of the nonlinear system , so that , with continuously differentiable in near , and let be the Jacobian of evaluated at that equilibrium.

Write for the eigenvalues of . Then exactly one of the following three situations occurs.

  • If for every , that is if is Hurwitz, then is locally asymptotically stable for the nonlinear system.
  • If for at least one , then is unstable for the nonlinear system.
  • If for every with equality for at least one of them, the test is inconclusive and nothing can be said about the stability of for the nonlinear system.

The eigenvalue test transfers to a nonlinear system through the Jacobian, and the conclusion is always local: even in the first case the theorem gives no estimate of how large the region of attraction is.

The third bullet is not laziness: on the imaginary axis the linear term neither grows nor decays, so the neglected remainder decides the outcome. Two systems with the same Jacobian can then behave in opposite ways.

Example: the Van der Pol equation

State space description

Equilibrium

Jacobian

Eigenvalues

The nonlinear system is L.A.S. for .

Remarks

When the nonlinear system is unstable, since the eigenvalues move into the right half plane.

When the original system reduces to a linear system and it is stable in the sense of Lyapunov.

Question 1: the Van der Pol origin is L.A.S. for . Is it G.A.S.?

No, and this is the standard warning about the indirect method.

The system has an unstable limit cycle surrounding the origin, at a radius of roughly 1.5 to 2 depending on , and trajectories starting outside it escape to infinity.

The region of attraction of the origin is the inside of that cycle, which is a bounded set.

Demo D8, immediately after this section, shows exactly that: start inside the cycle and the trajectory spirals into the origin as the linearization predicts, start outside it and the same system runs away, even though the Jacobian is unchanged.

The indirect method never gives a region of attraction, only the existence of some ball, which is why the direct method of Section 19 is needed for quantitative answers.

Question 2: give two scalar systems with the same Jacobian at the origin and opposite stability, to illustrate the third bullet.

Take the two cubic systems below.

Both have Jacobian , which sits exactly on the imaginary axis.

The first is asymptotically stable, since and always have opposite signs.

The second is unstable, since they always have the same sign and the state escapes in finite time.

The linearization is identical in both cases, so it cannot possibly decide between them.

Question 3: why does the theorem say L.A.S. rather than G.A.S. even when the Jacobian is strongly Hurwitz?

Because the Taylor expansion is only accurate near .

The bound on the remainder is a statement about the limit as , so it says nothing about a large perturbation.

Far from the equilibrium the neglected terms can dominate completely and send the state somewhere else, as the Van der Pol limit cycle does.

Making the Jacobian more strongly Hurwitz usually enlarges the region of attraction, but the method still cannot certify how large it is.

D8 Demo: Van der Pol stability analysis using Lyapunov's indirect method

The left plot is the true nonlinear flow, and the right plot compares one nonlinear trajectory against the prediction of its linearization.

Change the sign of to move the Jacobian eigenvalues across the imaginary axis and watch both panels react.

State plane: the nonlinear flow
Nonlinear against linearized prediction

Left plot: the amber curve is the selected trajectory, the faint grey curves are the fan of other starting points, the thin black circle is the unit circle where the damping changes sign, and the navy dot is the equilibrium. Right plot: of the true nonlinear system in blue against from the linearization in dashed red, both started from the same point.

Question 1: keep fixed and shrink the start radius. What happens to the gap between the two curves on the right?

The gap shrinks, and it shrinks faster than the trajectory itself.

That is precisely the remainder condition in the derivation.

For the Van der Pol system the neglected term is , which is cubic in the state.

Halving the start radius therefore divides the neglected term by about eight while the linear term only halves.

Question 2: push the start radius up towards its maximum with a positive . Where does the trajectory go, and what does the linearization say?

The nonlinear trajectory runs away and leaves every window, while the linearization still predicts a quiet decay to zero.

Both statements are correct in their own domain, and the disagreement is the whole point of the word local.

The damping coefficient is positive inside the strip and negative outside it, so energy is removed near the origin and added far from it.

The dividing line is an unstable limit cycle, at a radius of roughly 1.5 to 2 depending on , and it is the true boundary of the region of attraction.

Question 3: set to exactly zero. What does the theorem allow you to conclude?

Nothing at all, since the Jacobian eigenvalues are exactly and land on the imaginary axis.

This is the third bullet of the theorem in action.

In this particular case the full nonlinear system happens to reduce to the linear harmonic oscillator, so it is Lyapunov stable.

That conclusion comes from looking at the actual equations and not from the theorem, which is exactly what the theorem warns you about.

16 Stable and unstable subspaces of LTI systems

Notes on linear algebra: span and subspace

Span

If , the span of is the set of linear combinations of vectors of .

Subspace

A subspace is a subset of that is closed under linear combinations.

Every span is a subspace, and every subspace contains the origin.

Direct sum

The direct sum of two subspaces and is the set of all sums of a vector from each.

The symbol rather than an ordinary sum records that the two subspaces meet only at the origin, and in that case every vector of has exactly one such decomposition.

Question 1: is the set a subspace?

No, because it is not closed under multiplication by a negative scalar.

Take and , which gives outside the set.

Stable and unstable subspaces

Consider an LTI system with its solution written through the matrix exponential.

Definition

The stable subspace is defined as the following set.

In words, it is the set of initial conditions for which the state converges to zero.

Why it is spanned by eigenvectors

Recall the general modal form of the response.

If then every term attached to that eigenvalue dies.

Three consequences

Main result: the stable and unstable subspaces

Let be an LTI system on . Then the following three statements hold.

  1. The stable subspace is the span of all eigenvectors and generalized eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues with .
  2. The unstable subspace is the span of all eigenvectors and generalized eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues with .
  3. The two subspaces intersect only at the origin and together fill the whole space.

Every initial condition therefore splits in exactly one way into a part in and a part in , and the state converges to zero precisely when the second part is zero.

Example 1: a saddle in the plane

Eigenvalues

Stable eigenvector

Unstable eigenvector

What this looks like

In Demo D9 we will see that only initial states on the line decay, and everything else grows.

A couple of notes

Any initial condition that is not , that is not in , will grow.

Initial conditions corresponding to instability do not form a subspace.

Why not a subspace: take one growing initial condition and its own negative, both of which grow. Their sum is the zero vector, which decays, so the set is not closed under addition.

Example 2: a defective unstable pair in three dimensions

The stable direction

The unstable eigenvector

The generalized eigenvector

The first entry of can be any number, since adding a multiple of keeps the equation true.

The unstable subspace

So is the whole plane and is the axis.

Question 2: why is a subspace while the set of growing initial conditions is not?

Because the limit operation is linear and the number zero is closed under addition.

So a linear combination of decaying initial conditions still decays.

Growth has no such closure, since two growing terms can cancel each other exactly, as the note above shows.

Question 3: the definition of uses rather than . Why include the axis?

So that the direct sum covers the whole space with no gap.

Directions with do not converge to zero, so they cannot be in .

They must therefore be assigned to for the identity to hold.

Some texts split them off into a third space called the centre subspace, which is useful when studying marginal cases in more detail.

Question 4: what practical use does the stable subspace have if it has measure zero and no real system can start exactly on it?

It tells you which directions the controller has to fight and which ones it can leave alone.

The component of the state along takes care of itself, so control effort should go into the component.

It also explains why open loop stabilization of an unstable plant is hopeless in practice, since staying on would require infinite precision.

Balancing a broom on your hand is the everyday version, where the stable direction exists but feedback is the only way to remain near it.

Because the Jordan block couples the second coordinate into the first.

Question 3: the unstable subspace here has dimension two while the stable one has dimension one. Is that a coincidence of this matrix?

No, the dimensions are fixed by counting eigenvalues with multiplicity.

Here has algebraic multiplicity two so it contributes two dimensions, even though it supplies only one eigenvector.

The missing direction is filled by the generalized eigenvector, which is why the counting uses algebraic and not geometric multiplicity.

Almost every initial condition therefore grows, since the decaying set is only a line inside a three dimensional space.

19 Lyapunov's direct method

Positive definite functions

There is a method that decides stability without solving the differential equation at all.

Without loss of generality we can assume the equilibrium of a nonlinear system is the origin.

If , shift coordinates.

The shifted vector field satisfies , so is an equilibrium of the new system.

The two systems differ only by a translation of the state, so every stability property of for the original system is the same property of for the shifted one.

Definition: positive definite

A function is positive definite, written PD, given a neighbourhood of the origin , if two conditions hold.

The backslash is set minus, defined by .

Three related names

  • If the second condition is relaxed to for all , then is positive semi-definite, written PSD.
  • If is PD, then is negative definite, written ND.
  • If is PSD, then is negative semi-definite, written NSD.

Positive definite matrices

The same four words are used for matrices. A symmetric matrix is called positive definite, written , when the scalar is positive for every nonzero vector, and positive semi-definite, written , when it is never negative.

Negative definite and negative semi-definite matrices are defined through in the same way, and are written and .

Only the symmetric part of a matrix affects its quadratic form, because the antisymmetric part contributes zero, which is why is taken symmetric from the start.

For a symmetric matrix the sign can be read off the eigenvalues. Diagonalize with an orthogonal matrix and change variables to .

As ranges over all nonzero vectors so does , so the sum is positive for every such exactly when every is positive.

The connection with the function definitions is immediate for a quadratic function . It always satisfies , so it is a PD function exactly when is a PD matrix, and the same holds for PSD, ND and NSD. The neighbourhood plays no role here, since gives the same sign along every ray through the origin, so a quadratic form that is PD near the origin is PD on all of .

Positive definite matrices and functions

The matrix definitions are the function definitions specialised to quadratic forms, and for those the eigenvalues settle the question.

Question 1: is positive definite on ?

No, it is only positive semi-definite.

It vanishes on the whole line , not just at the origin.

One eigenvalue is zero, which matches the eigenvalue criterion for PSD rather than PD.

Question 2: why does the definition allow a neighbourhood rather than insisting on all of ?

Because most useful Lyapunov functions for nonlinear systems are only well behaved near the equilibrium.

The natural energy of a pendulum is one example.

This is positive definite for but vanishes again at , which is the same physical position.

Restricting to a neighbourhood keeps the definition usable and matches the local conclusions the method delivers.

Lyapunov functions

Definition

Consider a nonlinear system with , and let be a function with two properties.

Property (i): is PD, meaning for all and .

Property (ii): is NSD along the trajectory of the system.

Such a is known as a Lyapunov function.

The time varying case

In the case where also depends on , a function is a Lyapunov function under the following two conditions.

Remark: a Lyapunov function can be thought of as a generalized energy function for the system. The derivative condition then says the system never gains energy.

Question 3: the derivative is computed without solving for . How is that possible?

Because the chain rule replaces by the right hand side of the differential equation.

The result is a function of alone, with no reference to time or to any particular trajectory.

Checking a sign condition on that function is algebra, while solving the differential equation is usually impossible.

This trade is the entire appeal of the direct method.

Question 4: what does the level set picture look like when ?

The velocity vector never points outward across a level set of .

The gradient is the outward normal to the level set, so the condition is a statement about an angle.

A trajectory can therefore slide along a level set or move inward, but it can never cross outward.

Demo D11 draws exactly this picture with the level sets and the velocity arrows together.

The main theorem of the direct method

Part 1: Lyapunov stability

The origin is stable in the sense of Lyapunov if there exists a Lyapunov function .

The proof is short. For any trajectory , integrate the derivative.

So the whole trajectory lies inside the set , which is bounded.

It also shows that every level set is invariant.

Once a trajectory enters an invariant set it never leaves.

Part 2: asymptotic stability

If there exists a Lyapunov function and furthermore in an open neighbourhood of the origin, except for the origin itself, then the system is A.S. around the origin.

Part 3: global asymptotic stability

If Part 2 holds everywhere in , and whenever , then the system is G.A.S.

The second condition is called radial unboundedness.

Part 4: instability

If there exists that is PD, with also PD in an open neighbourhood of , then the system is unstable around .

Theorem: Lyapunov's direct method

Consider the system with continuously differentiable and , so that the origin is an equilibrium. Let be an open set containing the origin, and let be continuously differentiable with . The derivative of along the trajectories of the system is the function

A function that vanishes at the origin is called positive definite (PD) on if it is positive at every point of , negative definite (ND) if it is negative at every such point, and negative semi-definite (NSD) if it is never positive on . A function defined on all of is radially unbounded if as . Then:

  1. If is PD and is NSD on , the origin is stable in the sense of Lyapunov.
  2. If is PD and is ND on , the origin is asymptotically stable.
  3. If , is PD and radially unbounded, and is ND on , the origin is globally asymptotically stable.
  4. If a continuously differentiable with has both and PD on , the origin is unstable.

No trajectory is ever computed: every hypothesis is a sign condition on and on , which are functions of alone.

Necessary and sufficient, but not constructive: for asymptotic and global asymptotic stability the conditions of the theorem are necessary as well as sufficient. Converse Lyapunov theorems show that whenever the origin of , with continuously differentiable, is asymptotically stable, a satisfying Part 2 exists, and whenever it is globally asymptotically stable a radially unbounded satisfying Part 3 exists. Those proofs establish existence without constructing , however, and no method is guaranteed to find a Lyapunov function even for a system that is known to be stable: energy arguments, quadratic candidates, sum of squares programs and learning based searches are all best-effort. Failing to find one therefore proves nothing, since the failure may be the method's rather than the system's, and instability needs its own certificate from Part 4.

Question 5: take the example with . What do the level sets and the flow look like?

The level sets are circles of radius centred at the origin, called the contours of , and the sublevel sets are the filled discs they enclose.

The figure below uses a concrete flow for which this works, written in polar coordinates .

Both panels use the flow above with . The dashed grey circles are contours of , the green dots are the starting points, and the red circle is itself a trajectory, since there.

The left panel shows the filled disc . A trajectory that starts inside it stays inside, because can only decrease along the trajectory, which is the invariance argument of Part 1 drawn as a picture.

The right panel shows several contours. A trajectory started outside crosses them only inward, and then rides along the red circle , where and the flow is tangent to the contour.

No arrow ever points outward across a contour, which is the angle condition of Question 4 seen directly.

Linear systems: for an LTI system a Lyapunov function can be constructed systematically as a quadratic form , and Section 24 shows how.

Radial unboundedness: LAS but not GAS

Demo D12, which follows this section, provides a standard example that shows why Part 3 of the theorem needs radial unboundedness. It uses the function below together with the system written out in the demo.

This function is positive definite, and for the system of Demo D12 we have whenever .

The trouble is entirely in the shape of the level sets.

The threshold is , because the first term never exceeds one no matter how large becomes.

So a trajectory can have and while stays bounded.

Therefore is not radially unbounded, and the system is only L.A.S. and not G.A.S.

The lesson: a decreasing only confines the state when the sublevel sets are bounded. Radial unboundedness is precisely the condition that makes every sublevel set bounded.

Question 1: for the stable spiral, tilt until red segments appear. Is the system now unstable?

No, the system has not changed at all, only your choice of has.

The red segments mean this particular fails to be a Lyapunov function, not that the origin is unstable.

This is the one sidedness of the method: a bad candidate proves nothing.

Press the button that solves the Lyapunov equation and the red segments disappear, because a valid certificate always exists for a Hurwitz matrix.

Question 2: what does the button “Use the that solves the Lyapunov equation” actually compute?

It solves the Lyapunov equation for with .

This is a linear system of equations in the entries of , so it is solved directly rather than searched for.

When is Hurwitz, as for the stable spiral and the stable node, the solution is unique and positive definite, and certifies asymptotic stability.

The other two menu entries show what happens when is not Hurwitz.

For the unstable spiral the equation still has a unique solution, but that is negative definite, so the readout reports that is not a Lyapunov function. The same solve is still informative: is positive definite with , so Part 4 of the theorem proves the origin is unstable.

For the undamped centre the equation has no solution at all, because the eigenvalues sum to zero and the linear system for the entries of becomes singular. The button then falls back to , for which and everywhere, a Lyapunov function that proves stability in the sense of Lyapunov but not asymptotic stability.

Where the equation comes from, and why its solution behaves this way, is the subject of Section 24, which develops Lyapunov theory for LTI systems, with the equation itself derived in its subsection on the Lyapunov matrix equation.

Question 3: select the undamped centre with the identity . What do the contours and the right plot show?

The trajectory follows one contour exactly, and is constant in time.

This satisfies the NSD condition, so Part 1 applies and the origin is Lyapunov stable.

It fails the strict condition of Part 2, so nothing about asymptotic stability can be claimed, and indeed the trajectory never approaches the origin.

The physical reading is that is the conserved energy of an undamped oscillator.

The function used is the saturating candidate from the radial unboundedness part of Section 19.

It is positive definite on the whole plane, since both terms are non-negative and vanish together only at the origin, and its derivative along the system is negative everywhere except the origin.

What it lacks is radial unboundedness. The first term never reaches one, so for every , and stays bounded as with fixed. As a result the level sets with are open curves rather than closed ones.

The left plot draws the contours of over a wide window, and the right plot zooms into the unit square. A trajectory of the system is drawn on both, so you can watch it either converge or escape.

Question 1: press the escape button. What happens to along the escaping trajectory?

It decreases the whole time, exactly as the theory promises, but it settles at a positive limit instead of reaching zero.

The reason is that the first term of saturates at one as grows, while levels off at a nonzero constant.

For the escape preset that limit is about , reached from an initial value of about .

So is satisfied at every instant and the state still runs away.

This is the counterexample that the radial unboundedness condition exists to exclude.

Question 2: raise the contour slider past one. What changes about the bold curve?

It stops being a closed loop and splits into two branches that run off to the left and to the right.

Solving for makes this explicit.

For the quantity under the root becomes negative at a finite , which closes the curve.

For it stays positive for every , so the curve continues forever.

Question 3: in the zoomed plot the contours look like ordinary closed ovals, a textbook picture of asymptotic stability. What is the honest conclusion from it alone, and why is that not enough for G.A.S.?

That the origin is locally asymptotically stable, which is true.

Inside the unit square every contour with is a bounded oval, and any sublevel set contained in the window is bounded and invariant, so trajectories starting inside it converge. That is exactly what Part 2 of the theorem already delivers.

Part 3 is a claim about the whole plane, and nothing in the window says anything about starts outside it. The wide view shows that the contours with open up into two horizontal channels stretching to infinity, and a trajectory that starts in one of them can escape without ever violating .

The general lesson is that a Lyapunov certificate is only valid on the region where you actually checked its assumptions.

Question 4: what is the largest region of attraction this can certify?

Every sublevel set with is bounded, because forces . Each is also invariant, since , so every trajectory that starts in one converges to the origin.

The union of these sets is everything with , and that is the region the certificate covers.

The set is itself unbounded, a band along the axis that gets thinner as grows, even though every sublevel set inside it is bounded. The escape preset of Question 1 starts at , outside , which is why the certificate says nothing about it.

A different could certify a different region, since the region of attraction is a property of the system and not of the candidate function.

Question 5: can the certificate be repaired by making radially unbounded?

Removing the saturation from the first term gives a radially unbounded function, whose sublevel sets are all discs.

For this system, though, its derivative is not negative everywhere. At , for instance, it is positive.

In fact no repair can succeed for this system. If some radially unbounded had on , Part 3 of the theorem would make the origin G.A.S., and the escaping trajectory of Question 1 shows that it is not.

Making the level sets bounded and keeping the derivative negative are competing requirements in general, and here the system itself rules out meeting both.

The system

Where the derivative is negative

Strictly, is only negative semi-definite on the disc, because it vanishes on the axis, so Part 2 of the theorem does not apply exactly as stated. The conclusion still holds because a trajectory cannot stay on the line away from the origin: there , so the state leaves the line at once and resumes decreasing. This refinement of Part 2 is known as LaSalle's invariance principle.

Two definitions come first. For the system , a set is invariant if every solution that starts in stays in for all , and a set is positively invariant if every solution that starts in stays in for all .

Theorem: LaSalle's invariance principle

Let be locally Lipschitz on an open set , and let be a compact set that is positively invariant for . Let be continuously differentiable with for every . Define

Then every solution that starts in approaches as , in the sense that .

Unlike Part 2 of the direct method, only has to be non-positive, and the missing strictness is recovered from the dynamics through the invariant set .

The form used most often is a corollary for an equilibrium at the origin. If is positive definite on , on , and no solution other than can stay identically in , then the origin is asymptotically stable. If in addition and is radially unbounded, it is globally asymptotically stable.

For the Van der Pol equation, take with . It is compact, it lies inside the strip , and it is positively invariant because on it. There exactly when , so is the part of the axis inside . A solution that stays in has , hence and as well, so . Every solution that starts in therefore converges to the origin, and letting increase to one half covers the open unit disc.

Careful with the region: the strip is where has the right sign, but the strip itself is not invariant. The certified region is the largest sublevel set of that fits inside the strip, which is the disc of radius one.

Question 1: press “Start inside the certified disc”. Is monotonically decreasing, and why is the certified region the disc rather than the whole strip ?

Yes. The right plot shows falling the whole time, with touching zero each time the trajectory crosses , which flattens the decrease momentarily without ever reversing it.

That is what the certificate guarantees, and it can guarantee it only because the disc is a set the trajectory cannot leave. A sublevel set of is invariant whenever on it, and the sublevel sets that fit inside the strip are exactly the following.

With , letting increase to one half sweeps out the open disc of radius one.

The strip itself is not invariant. A trajectory that starts in it near with a very large drifts out of the strip into the region where has the wrong sign before it settles, so the strip cannot be certified.

Question 2: compare “Start between the disc and the cycle” with “Start beyond the limit cycle”. Both start outside the certified disc, so why do they end so differently, and does the difference mean the certificate is wrong?

In both cases rises and falls, because the trajectory alternates between the red region outside the strip, where energy is added, and the green region inside it, where energy is removed.

From the middle button the green passages still win overall, so the trajectory spirals back in and falls to zero. From the third button the red passages win instead and grows without bound.

The balance point between the two is an unstable limit cycle, sitting at a radius somewhere between about 1.5 and 2 depending on and on the direction, and it is the true boundary of the region of attraction. Over one period around it the energy gained and lost cancel exactly.

The certificate is not wrong, only conservative, which is the normal situation. A Lyapunov function gives a sufficient condition, so the disc it certifies is genuinely inside the region of attraction, but nothing forces it to be all of it, and the middle button shows starts a good deal further out still converging.

A different would certify a different subset, and modern methods search over families of polynomial to make the certified region as large as possible.

Question 3: set negative and start very close to the origin. What do you observe, and what does the theory say?

The colours swap, so the strip near the origin turns red, increases, and the trajectory spirals outward away from the origin.

The derivative has changed sign inside the strip.

So is positive definite and is non-negative near the origin. Because vanishes on the axis it is only positive semi-definite, so Part 4 does not apply exactly as stated, but the same observation as before settles it: no trajectory other than the origin can stay on the line , so keeps increasing and the origin is unstable.

This agrees with the indirect method, which puts the Jacobian eigenvalues in the right half plane for .

The outward spiral does not continue forever, because it settles onto a stable limit cycle where the red and green passages balance.

Question 1: where exactly did the argument use radial unboundedness?

In the step from asymptotic stability to global asymptotic stability.

Every sublevel set of this is a disc, so no trajectory can run off to infinity while decreases.

The derivative bound also holds on all of rather than on a neighbourhood, which is the other requirement of Part 3.

Both conditions of Part 3 are therefore met and the conclusion is global.

Question 2: the bound never says what and actually are. Why is that so useful?

Because one calculation covers an infinite family of systems at once.

Any saturation, any dead zone, any smooth curve staying inside the sector is allowed.

This is called robust stability, since the conclusion survives any uncertainty that respects the bound.

Real components are rarely known exactly, so a bound is often all the information available.

Question 3: why is the guaranteed envelope rather than something slower?

Because the derivative bound can be written directly in terms of itself.

With the bound derived above is exactly .

This is the comparison lemma, and it upgrades a qualitative conclusion into a decay rate.

Getting a rate out of a Lyapunov function is one of the main reasons the method is used in practice.

Question 4: suppose the sector bound has a larger gain, and with . Does the system become unstable? Raise the gain slider above one half with the linear shape to find out.
