The linear shape shows where the family really loses stability, since with the system is linear with explicit eigenvalues.

The system is asymptotically stable for , has an eigenvalue at zero when , and genuinely diverges for . The quadratic certificate reaches exactly the same threshold, so for this family it loses nothing.

Question 5: pick the saturating shape and raise the gain past one. Why does the state stop growing even though the origin is unstable?

Because flattens out for large while the term keeps growing.

Far from the origin the linear pull always wins, so every trajectory is eventually trapped in a bounded set.

The origin is still unstable, so the state settles onto some other attractor instead, typically a pair of new equilibria.

This is a good reminder that instability of an equilibrium and unboundedness of the state are different statements.

24 Lyapunov theory for LTI systems

The quadratic candidate

Everything so far applied to a general nonlinear system, and the Lyapunov function had to be guessed.

For a linear system the guessing stops, because one family of candidates always suffices.

Consider an LTI system.

Take the quadratic candidate below.

All eigenvalues of are then real positive numbers.

So is a legitimate positive definite function, and it is radially unbounded as well.

Now differentiate along the trajectories of the system.

The whole derivative collapsed into another quadratic form, and the matrix in the middle is what we name .

If , that is positive semidefinite, then the derivative has the right sign everywhere.

The key simplification is that for a linear system the sign condition on becomes a matrix inequality rather than a statement about a function of .

Question 1: why can we assume is symmetric with no loss of generality?

Because the antisymmetric part of any matrix contributes nothing to a quadratic form.

Split with and .

So only the symmetric part is visible to , and we may as well take symmetric from the start.

Question 2: where exactly did the calculation use the fact that the system is linear?

At the substitution , which turned the product rule into a matrix expression.

For a nonlinear system the same candidate gives the following instead.

That is no longer a quadratic form, and its sign has to be checked by hand region by region.

The linear case is the one case where the check reduces to a finite matrix condition.

Question 3: for a scalar system , what do and become?

Both are single positive numbers, and the equation reads as follows.

A positive requires when , which is exactly the stability condition.

The general theorem below is the matrix version of this one line.

The Lyapunov matrix equation

Definition: Lyapunov matrix equation

Linear in the unknown even though appears twice, so it is equations in the same number of unknowns.

Theorem
  1. For , if there exists that solves , then is stable in the sense of Lyapunov.
  2. For , if there exists that solves , then is asymptotically stable, and in fact globally asymptotically stable because is radially unbounded.
  3. If is Hurwitz, then for every there exists a unique that solves .

Parts one and two are the direct method with a quadratic , and part three is the converse that makes the equation a usable test.

Parts one and two are the direct method specialised to a quadratic , so they need no new proof.

Part three is the converse statement, and it is the reason the Lyapunov equation is useful in practice.

It says we may pick any positive definite we like, solve a linear system, and read stability off the sign of .

Proof of part three: the integral formula for

Parts one and two need no new proof, but part three does. It promises a unique positive definite solution whenever is Hurwitz, and the proof writes that solution down explicitly.

The integral converges because every entry of decays exponentially when is Hurwitz.

Proof

Define the integrand as a matrix valued function of time.

Differentiate it, using for the second term.

Now integrate both sides from zero to infinity.

The left side used , which is where the Hurwitz assumption enters.

Recognising the integral as gives the Lyapunov equation.

It remains to check that is positive definite.

Since is positive definite and is nonsingular for every , the integrand is positive definite for every , so is positive definite.

Finally, the solution is unique. If and both solve the equation, their difference satisfies , and therefore

So is constant in time. It equals at and tends to zero as , which forces .

Question 4: what does the integral formula mean if ?

Then is the total squared energy of the free response started at .

So the Lyapunov function is not an arbitrary certificate, it is the cost still to be paid from the current state.

It decreases along trajectories because part of the cost has already been spent, which is the cleanest intuition for why .

Replacing by a general weights the states, and adding a control cost turns this into the linear quadratic regulator.

Question 5: why does require to be Hurwitz rather than merely stable?

A marginally stable system has bounded but not decaying, so does not tend to zero.

The integral then diverges and no finite exists.

The undamped oscillator is the standard example, and it matches the fact that the linear map is singular there.

Strict decay of every mode is what makes the total cost finite.

Using the theorem as a test

In practice the theorem is used as a recipe: choose a positive definite , usually , solve for , and check whether is positive definite.

The system is asymptotically stable if and only if the solution exists and is positive definite, so the whole test is one linear solve and one symmetric eigenvalue check.

How the linear solve is actually carried out is not needed for the rest of this page, but here are the standard ways of doing it.

  • Vectorize. Stacking the columns of into one long vector turns the equation into an ordinary linear system with unknowns, written with the Kronecker product .
    The eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix are the sums of eigenvalues of , so it is invertible exactly when no two of them sum to zero. This is easy to code, but a dense solve of that size costs on the order of operations, so it only suits small systems.
  • Bartels–Stewart. An orthogonal change of coordinates brings to its (quasi) triangular Schur form, . In those coordinates the equation becomes with , which is solved entry by entry by substitution before transforming back. The cost is on the order of , and this is the method numerical libraries use.
  • Semidefinite programming. Instead of fixing , search directly for any with , a linear matrix inequality that a convex solver such as CVX or CVXPY can handle. It is slower than solving the equation, but the same formulation extends to uncertain systems where no single equation is available.

The integral formula above also produces , but it is mainly a proof device, since evaluating the integral numerically is slower and less accurate than any of these.

Library routines implement Bartels–Stewart. Their conventions differ from the form used here, so pay attention to the transpose.

% MATLAB, Control System Toolbox: lyap(A, Q) solves A*X + X*A' + Q = 0
P = lyap(A', Q);                  % so this solves A'*P + P*A + Q = 0
isStable = all(eig(P) > 0);
# Python, SciPy: solve_continuous_lyapunov(a, q) solves a X + X a^H = q
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_continuous_lyapunov
P = solve_continuous_lyapunov(A.T, -Q)          # A^T P + P A = -Q
is_stable = np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(P) > 0)
# Python, python-control: control.lyap(A, Q) solves A X + X A^T + Q = 0
import control
P = control.lyap(A.T, Q)                         # A^T P + P A + Q = 0

When two eigenvalues of sum to zero the equation is singular, and a library call either stops with an error or returns a numerically meaningless result, so it is worth checking the residual as well as the sign of .

Note. Failure to find a Lyapunov function does not necessarily imply instability if one starts with but not .

Guessing and computing can produce an indefinite for a perfectly stable system, and all we learn is that this particular guess was a bad one.

Starting from and solving for is the direction that never wastes effort.

Question 6: when does the Lyapunov equation fail to have a unique solution?

Exactly when for some pair of eigenvalues of , including the case .

The eigenvalues of the linear map are precisely the sums .

So a pole at the origin, or a purely imaginary conjugate pair, makes the map singular.

A Hurwitz has every eigenvalue strictly in the left half plane, so no such sum can vanish, which is part three of the theorem.

Question 7: the theorem is stated as an existence result. How is it used as a test?

Turn it around: fix and solve for .

If the solution exists and is positive definite, part two gives global asymptotic stability.

If the solution exists but is not positive definite, then by part three cannot be Hurwitz, so the system is not asymptotically stable.

This turns a stability question into one linear solve and one eigenvalue check on a symmetric matrix, which is numerically very reliable.

Question 8: we already have the eigenvalue test and Routh-Hurwitz. Why bother with a matrix equation?

Because it produces a certificate, not just a yes or no answer.

The matrix gives an explicit function whose level sets are invariant sets of the flow.

That certificate survives perturbation, so the same often proves stability for a whole family of nearby systems.

It is also the computational core of the linear quadratic regulator and of many robustness tests, where the eigenvalues alone are not enough.

Question 9: give a concrete case where guessing gives a useless answer for a stable system.

Take the stable system below and guess .

That has determinant , so it is indefinite and the test says nothing.

Yet both eigenvalues of are at , so the system is asymptotically stable.

The energy in the naive coordinates grows for a while before decaying, which is transient growth, and the fix is to choose first and let the solve find the right .

Worked example: the damped second order system

Take the classical damped second order equation.

Choosing and gives the state space representation.

The eigenvalues follow from the characteristic polynomial .

If then is Hurwitz, so a positive definite must exist.

A first guess that is not sharp enough

Try the obvious candidate below, which is the sum of squares.

Compute the left side of the Lyapunov equation.

The matrix is positive semidefinite but not positive definite.

We can know Lyapunov stability from this, but not asymptotic stability.

A second guess that works

Take the sharper candidate below, with .

Differentiating along the trajectories gives the following.

Every cross term cancels, and what is left is negative definite.

In matrix form the second candidate corresponds to the pair below.

Both are positive definite for , since , so part two of the theorem gives global asymptotic stability.

Question 10: the first candidate gave on the whole line . Does the system actually stall there?

No, it passes straight through.

On that line the velocity is zero but the acceleration is not, since whenever .

So no trajectory can stay on the set where vanishes, other than the origin itself.

That observation is exactly the invariance principle, which upgrades the first candidate from stability to asymptotic stability without needing the second one.

Question 11: where did the second candidate come from?

It is what the solve produces when you set and run the Lyapunov matrix equation of Section 24.

The rewriting as is a completion of the square on that .

Expanding the bracketed form gives exactly this, which confirms the two expressions agree.

The lesson is that a clever guess is usually a solve in disguise.

Question 12: what happens to both candidates when ?

The first gives , so everywhere and the level sets are exactly the trajectories.

That is the correct certificate for the undamped oscillator, which is stable in the sense of Lyapunov but not asymptotically stable.

The second gives too, and collapses to the identity, so the two candidates coincide.

No positive definite is available at , which matches part three of the theorem failing when is not Hurwitz.

28 Summary of the module

Stability is a property of a nominal trajectory, and Lyapunov's definition makes it precise: whatever tolerance is named first, a starting radius can be found that keeps the perturbation within it.

Asymptotic stability adds convergence on top of that, and it comes in a local and a global flavour.

The definitions, and the linear special case

For linear systems the nominal trajectory drops out, so the whole system is stable or not, and the local and global versions coincide.

The tests, in the order they were introduced

The five tests
  • Eigenvalue test for LTI systems, using and, for marginal eigenvalues, the number of eigenvectors.
  • Routh-Hurwitz test, which decides whether every root of has negative real part from its coefficients alone, without computing any root.
  • Lyapunov's indirect method, which transfers the eigenvalue test to a nonlinear system through the Jacobian, and gives only a local conclusion.
  • Lyapunov's direct method, which certifies stability with a generalized energy function and can reach global conclusions.
  • The Lyapunov matrix equation , which specialises the direct method to LTI systems and turns the search for a certificate into a single linear solve.

The eigenvalue test, Routh-Hurwitz and the Lyapunov matrix equation are exact tests for LTI systems. The indirect method carries the eigenvalue test over to nonlinear systems, but only locally and with an inconclusive case, while the direct method works for nonlinear systems in general: a Lyapunov function exists whenever the origin is asymptotically stable, but no method is guaranteed to find one.

The verdicts, side by side

Every line is a way of answering the same question, and they differ only in what they need as input and how strong a conclusion they return.

The structural picture

The stable subspace collects the directions that decay and the unstable subspace collects the rest.

Stable and unstable subspaces

Each is spanned by the eigenvectors and generalized eigenvectors of its own group of eigenvalues, so the split is read straight off the eigenstructure of .

The three traps to remember

Three traps

A marginal eigenvalue is only safe when it is non-defective. A Jacobian whose rightmost eigenvalues sit on the imaginary axis needs another tool, such as the direct method. A decreasing only confines the state when its sublevel sets are bounded, so a that is not radially unbounded says nothing about starts far away, even if the system happens to be G.A.S.

Final question: you are handed a nonlinear model and asked whether an operating point is stable. What is a sensible order of attack?

Find the equilibria first, since stability is always a statement about one of them, and shift the operating point to the origin.

Linearize there and test the Jacobian, either through its eigenvalues or through Routh-Hurwitz if the model has symbolic parameters.

If the Jacobian is Hurwitz the operating point is locally asymptotically stable, and if it has an eigenvalue with positive real part it is unstable. Either way Lyapunov's indirect method settles the yes or no question.

The indirect method never says how far from the operating point the state may start and still return. For that, and for the inconclusive case where the rightmost eigenvalues sit on the imaginary axis, use Lyapunov's direct method to find a certificate. Pick a candidate , for instance the quadratic with solving the Lyapunov matrix equation for the Jacobian . Compute along the nonlinear dynamics, and find the largest level for which the sublevel set is bounded and on except at the origin.

That sublevel set is invariant, and every trajectory that starts in it converges to the operating point, so it is a certified inner estimate of the region of attraction, in the same way as the disc certified for the Van der Pol equation in Demo D13.

Finally, compare the size of the certified region with the disturbances the system will actually see, because a local result with a tiny region is not an engineering answer.
